text: A café promo. Eleven must-have shots. Two people, one afternoon on location.
The crew packs up at five forty. At eleven that night, the editor finds that every pour cuts away after two seconds, and nobody filmed a customer drinking.
Editing apps can already find a cup in your footage. Their documentation doesn't describe checking the shot list: how long, how many takes, what must share the frame.
This is SceneGap Edge. It helps you check your shot list against your footage, on your own computer, before you leave.
You write the shot list in Chinese, the way the crew talks. Then you check the English phrase the model searches with, and add rules: minimum length, number of takes, what must appear together.
Point it at the camera card. It finds the cuts, keeps the original timecode, and makes one frame per second searchable with CLIP.
Every shot gets an answer from the AI, and a separate answer from you. Only yours counts.

Coffee or latte art poured into a cup, three seconds. The first candidate is an espresso stream with no cup in frame, so you reject it and say why. The next one is a latte-art pour. One click, accepted.

For the grinder, the AI still offers candidates, but they show tamping, not grinding. Nobody drinks coffee in these clips either. Both go on the reshoot list, with the reason, while the crew is still on location.
Here is the reshot clip. Only the new file is analysed. The grinder shot now has a real match. Accept it, and it comes off the reshoot list.

We tested on forty-four openly licensed clips, labelled by two separate AI annotators, and scored the held-out set once. The right clip was in the top five for seven of eleven shots; plain frame search got eight. On twelve controlled cases, the rule checks were right ten times. On a fresh, preregistered set of photo clips, a second check caught two thirds of the missing shots, with under four percent wrong reshoot calls.
Next, the image half of the model moves onto the ASUS UGen300. Today, analysis takes a little over two seconds per minute of footage on a desktop graphics card.
SceneGap Edge. Fewer surprises in the edit.
